report:
Evidence on CoQ10 for statin-associated muscle symptoms is mixed, and the answer is not simply "yes."

**Randomized trials with rigorous designs tend to show no benefit.** In a well-designed crossover trial that confirmed myalgia recurred specifically with statin (not placebo) rechallenge, CoQ10 supplementation did not reduce muscle pain, weakness, or aerobic performance issues compared with placebo (https://www.atherosclerosis-journal.com/article/S0021-9150(14)01636-0/fulltext, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4298455/). Another double-blind placebo-controlled study similarly found myalgia decreased over time in both groups with no difference attributable to CoQ10 (https://openaccesspub.org/article/273/jpmc-15-704.pdf). A 2018 updated meta-analysis in the *Journal of the American Heart Association*, pooling 12 RCTs (n=575), concluded there was no significant benefit of CoQ10 for statin-induced myopathy, calling for larger, better-designed trials (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/JAHA.118.009835; also summarized at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9495827/).

**Some meta-analyses and smaller studies report benefit.** Other analyses, sometimes citing the same or overlapping trial data, report CoQ10 significantly reduces pain, weakness, and cramps, and one recent study (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12536858/) found improved pain scores and creatine kinase with 50mg twice-daily dosing.

**Bottom line:** The evidence is conflicting and inconsistent across studies. The most methodologically rigorous randomized trials—those confirming true statin-related myalgia via crossover rechallenge—generally show no significant effect of CoQ10, while some other trials and meta-analyses report modest benefits. Overall, the claim that CoQ10 "relieves" statin muscle discomfort is not well-supported by the highest-quality evidence; it remains unproven and results are inconsistent rather than clearly affirmative.
